summary: This document defines basic classes of Logical Function Blocks (LFBs) for Forwarding and Control Element Separation (ForCES). They follow the ForCES forwarding element model and protocol specifications and cover typical router functions. The library includes descriptions and XML definitions.

eli5.summary: A router's jobs are broken into building blocks. This is the starter set of blocks, like a LEGO kit for routers.

subtitle: The starter kit of standard building blocks for describing a router's packet processing in ForCES.

tldr.problem: ForCES separates the control plane from the forwarding hardware, but the FE model alone only says how to describe a forwarding function. Vendors need a shared set of well-defined blocks to build a typical router from.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a base library of Logical Function Block (LFB) classes in XML, grouped into Ethernet processing, IP validation, IP forwarding, redirect and general-purpose blocks, plus the shared base types and metadata they use.
tldr.outcome: A Control Element can wire these blocks into a topology for IPv4 or IPv6 unicast forwarding over Ethernet and manage them over the ForCES protocol. Coverage is deliberately limited, with other media, multicast and richer schedulers left for later.

today: RFC 6956 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is the base LFB library for ForCES, built on RFC 5812.

sections.title: What the LFB Library Is
sections.content:
In the ForCES framework (RFC 3746), Control Elements (CEs) configure and manage separate Forwarding Elements (FEs) inside a Network Element using the ForCES protocol (RFC 5810). The FE model (RFC 5812) describes FE resources as classes of Logical Function Blocks (LFBs) and provides an XML schema for defining them.

RFC 6956 conforms to that model and defines the detailed LFB classes, including their XML. Together they form a base library meant to be combined into an LFB topology for a typical router doing IP forwarding. The RFC stresses that an LFB abstracts a function rather than an implementation, so that separate CEs and FEs can interoperate. More classes may be developed later, and vendors may define proprietary ones.

An LFB class is identified by a class ID and an instance by an instance ID. Metadata carries per-packet state from one LFB to another and is never sent across the network. An LFB has input and output ports, either singleton ports or group ports with indexed instances.
sections.eli5: A router is split into a boss (the CE) and workers (the FE). The workers are made of small blocks, and this RFC defines the standard blocks the boss can ask for.

sections.title: Scope, Design Choices and Groups
sections.content:
The library is scoped to what RFC 1812 expects of a typical router: framing and unframing packets for the attached network, validating and forwarding datagrams, choosing a next hop from a routing database, and exposing management and statistics. It deals only with Ethernet media and follows the weak-host model of RFC 1122.

Three design principles shaped the blocks. If one function can be built as one LFB or as two or more at the same cost, choose two or more for flexibility. Keep each LFB independent with minimal coupling. Do not define two LFBs for the same processing unless their functions clearly differ.

The blocks fall into five groups: Ethernet processing, IP packet validation, IP forwarding, redirect, and general purpose. Section 7 gives two worked use cases.
sections.eli5: The kit follows a few rules: small pieces that do one thing, pieces that do not depend much on each other, and no two pieces that do the same job.

sections.title: Base Types: Data, Frames and Metadata
sections.content:
A separate XML file called BaseTypeLibrary defines the shared types, built on the atomic types of the FE model. It adds atomic types such as IPv4Addr, IPv6Addr, IEEEMAC and VlanIDType, compound structs for table entries and statistics, and compound arrays for tables such as the IPv4 prefix table. Counters are plain unsigned integers that increase until they wrap around to zero; handling discontinuities is left to implementations.

Frame types say what packet an LFB port expects or emits: EthernetII, ARP, IPv4, IPv6, the unicast and multicast variants of IPv4 and IPv6, and Arbitrary.

Metadata types carry per-packet state between blocks. The library defines fifteen, such as PHYPortID (1), HopSelector (10) and ExceptionID (11). By default metadata produced by upstream blocks passes through all downstream blocks, even those that do not use it.
sections.eli5: Blocks pass packets along with little sticky notes, such as which port it came from. This part lists the kinds of notes and the shared labels all blocks agree on.

sections.title: Ethernet and Validation Blocks
sections.content:
Five Ethernet blocks cover the path from wire to IP. EtherPHYCop models a copper Ethernet interface, with link speed and duplex settings that default to auto-negotiation, and emits a PHYPortID metadata. EtherMACIn does the MAC-layer checks: it either runs in promiscuous mode or drops packets that fail the locality check against the local MAC addresses, and it has an optional L2 bridging output. EtherClassifier decapsulates frames and uses the VlanInputTable and EtherDispatchTable to assign a logical port and send each packet to the output for IPv4, IPv6, ARP and so on. EtherEncap looks up MediaEncapInfoIndex in its EncapTable to attach the MAC addresses and optional VLAN tag. EtherMACOut is the output counterpart of EtherMACIn and hands frames to the physical block.

Two validator blocks check IP packets. IPv4Validator follows RFC 1812 and sends valid packets to IPv4UnicastOut or IPv4MulticastOut. Packets needing more work, such as expired TTL or router alert options, leave through ExceptionOut; packets that are broken, such as a wrong version or bad checksum, leave through FailOut. IPv6Validator does the same under RFC 2460.
sections.eli5: These blocks are the front door of the router. They take the signal off the cable, check the packet is addressed to this router, work out what kind of packet it is, and throw out the broken ones.

sections.title: IP Forwarding Blocks
sections.content:
Unicast forwarding is split into two steps, each in IPv4 and IPv6 flavors. The IPv4UcastLPM block uses the packet's destination address as a key in its IPv4PrefixTable and produces a hop selector metadata from the longest prefix match. Table entries carry an ECMP flag and a default route flag, which give hooks for equal-cost multipath and reverse path forwarding, but the RFC says full ECMP or RPF would need additional blocks.

The IPv4NextHop block uses the hop selector as a table index and applies the result: it decrements TTL, recalculates the IP checksum, and sends the packet out on the output port chosen by the matching entry along with L3PortID and MediaEncapInfoIndex metadata. Exceptions include an invalid hop selector, a failed next-hop lookup, and an outgoing MTU smaller than the packet. IPv6UcastLPM and IPv6NextHop do the same for IPv6. Multicast forwarding is not defined by this library.
sections.eli5: One block looks up the destination in the router's address book and writes down which entry matched. The next block follows that entry to decide where the packet goes next.

sections.title: Redirect and General-Purpose Blocks
sections.content:
RedirectIn and RedirectOut carry packets between the FE and the CE using ForCES redirect messages. RedirectIn has only an output group port and requires a RedirectIndex metadata that selects the output instance; a packet without it is dropped. RedirectOut has only an input and delivers packets, with their remaining metadata, to the CE. For example, a packet that EtherEncap cannot resolve can be redirected so the CE can do ARP or neighbor discovery and update the table.

BasicMetadataDispatch sends a packet to an output port instance based on the value of one chosen metadata, using a table where the metadata value is a 32-bit integer. GenericScheduler is a preliminary scheduler that connects each input port instance to a queue; the only scheduling discipline defined is Round Robin, which is the default. More complex schedulers may inherit from it.
sections.eli5: Some packets need the boss to look at them, so there are blocks to send them up and bring them back. Other blocks act as a sorting station or a fair turn-taking line.

sections.title: Use Cases: IPv4 Forwarding and ARP
sections.content:
In the IPv4 forwarding example, each EtherPHYCop feeds an EtherMACIn and then an EtherClassifier. IPv4 packets go to IPv4Validator, unicast packets to IPv4UcastLPM, then IPv4NextHop, then EtherEncap, then BasicMetadataDispatch, which fans out to the right EtherMACOut using the L3PortID metadata.

In the ARP example, the CE does ARP processing. ARP packets from the classifier are redirected to the CE through RedirectOut, IPv4 packets lacking address resolution go the same way, and ARP packets from the CE come in through RedirectIn and are dispatched to the right output port. The RFC says these are examples only, not the only way to build router functions.
sections.eli5: Here the RFC shows the blocks snapped together like a pipeline, from the cable in to the cable out, and a side path that asks the boss when the router does not yet know a neighbor's address.

sections.title: IANA and Security Considerations
sections.content:
IANA created a registry of ForCES LFB class names and identifiers, and this document registers the LFBs it defines. The registration procedure is Standards Action for the range 0 to 65535 and First Come First Served with a public specification above 65535. The document also defines namespaces for Metadata ID, Exception ID and Validate Error ID, and keeps a metadata ID range reserved for private use.

For security, the RFC adds nothing new. The LFBs have the same security properties as other LFBs, so the mechanisms of the ForCES protocol (RFC 5810), including those of the SCTP-based transport mapping (RFC 5811), apply. ForCES protocol entities must be authenticated before they can access the information elements defined here.
sections.eli5: The block names and numbers go in an official list so nobody picks the same number twice, and only authenticated bosses and workers may talk to each other.
